# Analysis plan

This chapter was written before any outcome was examined. Changes made
after that point are marked where they occur, and each is logged in the
decision record with its reason and timing.

## Estimands

| Question | Population | Outcome | Summary measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | All randomized patients with an outcome | Any sore throat at rest, thirty minutes | Odds ratio, licorice vs sugar |
| Secondary | Same | Any sore throat across the four assessments | Population-averaged odds ratio, common to all assessments |
| Secondary (*added after review*, D-009) | Same | Any sore throat at each assessment | Population-averaged odds ratio at each assessment |

## Models

1. **Primary analysis.** Proportions by arm and an unadjusted logistic
   regression at thirty minutes (D-001, D-002).
2. **Repeated measures, population-averaged.** Logistic GEE with an
   exchangeable working correlation and robust standard errors, giving one
   odds ratio common to the four assessments (D-003). *Added after review
   (D-009):* a treatment-by-time model for the odds ratio at each
   assessment.
3. **Repeated measures, patient-level.** Logistic mixed model with a random
   intercept per patient. Reported beside the GEE because its odds ratio
   answers a different question (D-004). *Amended after review (D-008):*
   fitted by adaptive quadrature rather than the Laplace default.
4. **Sensitivity.** The primary model adjusted for sex, age, BMI, smoking,
   ASA status and surgery size (D-007). Interpreted as a conditional odds
   ratio, not a check of the unadjusted one.
5. **Missing outcomes.** Complete case, with best- and worst-case bounds
   (D-006).

## Verification before trusting a model

Each model function must recover a known effect from simulated data with
the same structure before it is run on the trial data
(`tests/testthat/test-models.R`).

## Reporting

Odds ratios with 95% CI from Wald intervals; p-values to three decimals.
Secondary results are descriptive; no multiplicity adjustment is planned
because there is a single primary comparison.
